newsitem.title: UK: Dollar mixed in Europe, spotlight on EMU and trade.
newsitem.headline: Dollar mixed in Europe, spotlight on EMU and trade.

text.p: The dollar had mixed fortunes in early Europe, slipping against the yen as market thoughts turned to trade but underpinned versus the mark as players betted on accord on the EMU stability pact at the EU summit in Amsterdam.
Analysts said an EU deal would bolster dollar/mark as it fanned speculation of a weak single currency, but dollar upside would be limited since agreement deal was now largely priced in.

Dollar/yen, however, was expected to remain capped as the spotlight shone on the contrasting trade situations in the U.S. and Japan ahead of the Group of Seven (G7) summit in Denver on June 20-22. Both countries release trade data this week.
The dollar was at 1.7360/70 marks and 114.10/20 yen at 0744 GMT versus 1.7365/75 and 114.65/75 in late Europe on Friday.
The market's conflicting impulses were reflected in the mark/yen cross, which fell to 65.71/73 from Friday's 65.99/02.

Ahead of the trade data on Tuesday and Thursday, the market was keenly awaiting tomorrow's U.S. May CPI after figures released on Friday showed May producer prices fell 0.3 percent. That confounded forecasts of a modest rise, and dampened speculation the Federal Reserve would tighten next month.
"Expectations about the next FOMC are definitely shifting into the camp of no policy move," said Stephen Hannah at IBJ.

Though that ought to upset a dollar which drew strength not so long ago from the prospect of higher interest rates, the positive reaction from U.S. asset markets should help the currency, said Hannah, who is director of research at IBJ.
U.S. stocks and bonds rallied strongly on Friday, enthused by a combination of the benign PPI data and a further rise in consumer sentiment in June. That boosted the dollar.

In Europe, the focus was firmly on the two-day Amsterdam summit starting today. Comments from European officials raised hopes of accord on the so-called stability pact -- designed to stop countries running big deficits after EMU begins.
"All eyes are on Amsterdam - that's going to overshadow any data from the U.S. for the next couple of days," said Elizabeth Cheale, trader at Dresdner Bank in London.
A dealer at a U.S. bank here reported some dollar selling in early trade, but said the U.S. unit remained attractive given the likelihood of accord on the stability pact.

"It looks as if they're going to reach agreement today or tomorrow, which makes a softer euro more likely. That means there is a lack of confidence in the mark and is making the dollar, French franc and Swiss franc all the more attractive," he said.
The French and Swiss units were broadly steady against the mark in morning Europe as players awaited summit news.

The next big international meeting after Amsterdam is the three-day G7 summit in Denver, Colorado, which begins on Friday. Dollar/yen dived to six-month lows last week amid concern that the summit would see trade friction between the U.S. and Japan, but recovered as those nerves ebbed.
"It appears trade is not going to be a big focus (at G7). It may be a discussion point, but I don't think it's going to be right at the top of the agenda," said Hannah at IBJ.
Late Tuesday night sees the release of data which economists expect to show Japan's May trade surplus widening to 548.5 billion yen from 229 billion last time.
U.S. April international trade figures due Thursday are predicted to show the deficit there increasing to $10 billion from $8.5 billion.
